subject: First-wave release polish: Docent's own MCP endpoint, zero-setup agent wiring, follow-up-review loop
thesis: Release-day pass with one goal: a new user must succeed on the first try. The heart of the change is the MCP story, which went through three designs in a day — each killed by a fact we verified along the way. It started as "warn when the IDE MCP server is off", became "flip Agent Workbench's hidden auto-wiring key" (rejected: unexposed default with unknown blast radius), then "inject an additive --mcp-config pointing at the public IDE server" (rejected: 119 tools, duplicated wholesale when the user's own config already registers that server), and landed on Docent's own MCP endpoint: the IDE's private MCP server, auth-token protected, filtered to exactly the 8 docent_* tools — and independent of the user-facing "Enable MCP server" setting, which is therefore no longer a prerequisite at all. Around it: both providers (Claude and Codex, both mechanisms verified against the live CLIs) get the endpoint injected per launch with zero user config; the post-review gray area gets a v1 loop that reuses the existing on-demand machinery; CI is anchored on a reproducible EAP; and the README now speaks to a first-time user. Everything compiles and builds at 0.4.1, but the new launch wiring has not yet been click-tested in a live IDE — that's the reviewer's biggest lever here.

sections.headline: Docent gets its own MCP endpoint — 8 tools, own port, no prerequisites
sections.narration: The silent first-run failure: on a fresh machine, a workbench-launched agent never sees the docent_* tools — nothing is recorded, the panel stays empty, no error anywhere in our surfaces. (Agent Workbench does offer its own "set up MCP" bubble, but it writes a user-level client config entry with a baked-in port — manual, per-user, per-client, and Docent itself gave no hint.) The fix is a dedicated endpoint: DocentMcpEndpoint parks a long-lived authorized session on the IDE's private MCP server — separate port, per-IDE-run auth token, tool filter reduced to the docent toolset. This resolves the reviewer's core objection to pointing agents at the public IDE server (~119 tools, duplicated in full when the user's own config already registers it), and it has a decisive side effect discovered in the MCP plugin's source: the private server runs regardless of the user-facing "Enable MCP server" setting, so that setting stopped being a first-run prerequisite entirely. The onboarding surfaces built earlier in the day were then demoted to what they should be: a project-open activity arms the endpoint (pre-warming the server before any launch), and the warning notice + balloon fire only in the genuine double-failure case — endpoint failed AND the public fallback is off.

comments.body: The honest risk of this change: authorizedSession lives in the MCP plugin's impl package and its doc says it "runs only for the method execution period" — we stretch that to IDE-lifetime by parking the block on awaitCancellation(). The semantics hold by design (the private server stays up while any session holds it, ref-counted), but a future MCP plugin update could change them. That's why the launch side keeps a fallback ladder (next section) and failure here logs at WARN instead of breaking anything.

The token returned by authorizedSession is only valid while the block runs, so the block must outlive every agent that got the token injected. App-service scope cancellation (IDE shutdown) is the natural end. After an IDE restart the token is dead — but injection happens per launch, so relaunched agents always carry the fresh one. An agent session that outlives the IDE loses the endpoint; same story as the public server's port drift, accepted.

Two non-obvious facts baked in here: (1) McpToolFilter is a sealed interface — it cannot be implemented outside its module; TextMcpToolFilter is the deliberately-open extension point. (2) The name it matches is fullyQualifiedName = toolset class FQN + "." + method (verified in the MCP plugin's reflection util), not the bare docent_record_decision — hence the package prefix, which also future-proofs against new docent tools.

The first caller pays the private server's ktor startup (the launch contributor calls this on the launch path). 10s is deliberately generous: a false-negative here silently downgrades the launch to the public-server fallback, which is exactly the 119-tool exposure we're trying to avoid.

OK now means "agents can reach the tools by either rung": the armed endpoint, or the public server as fallback. The enable-server one-click fix survives because it restores rung two when rung one is broken.

Reflection is not paranoia here — McpServerSettings is Kotlin-internal, so a direct call doesn't compile even though the JVM signatures are public (verified via javap before choosing this route). Side benefit: the platform-clean core (the nav panel imports McpPrereq) never links against the optional MCP plugin.

Arming at project open does double duty: the private server is warm before the first agent launch, and it makes the status surfaces truthful — without this, a fresh IDE with the public setting off would show a scary "agents can't reach the Docent" notice that a launch would in fact have fixed.

anchors.label: Prerequisite notice on the empty surface

comments.body: The notice lives at the top of the no-trail surface — where a confused first-time user actually looks — not only in a dismissable balloon. After the endpoint work it should almost never appear; when it does, something is genuinely broken and the one-click "Turn on the MCP server" restores the fallback injection path.

sections.headline: Zero-setup launch wiring for both providers — and the two designs it replaced
sections.narration: The launch contributor now injects the endpoint into every workbench agent launch, additively — the user's own MCP config is never touched, replaced, or shadowed. This section carries the day's full decision arc, because two credible designs were implemented and then rejected on verified facts. Design 1: flip Agent Workbench's agent.workbench.mcp.use.direct.http registry key so AWB itself wires MCP — rejected by the reviewer because the key is unexposed and defaulted off by JetBrains (unknown blast radius), and because its --strict-mcp-config semantics hide the user's globally-configured MCP servers from workbench sessions (verified: this machine's wiring lives in the global ~/.claude.json, exactly what strict mode would drop). Design 2: additive injection pointing at the public IDE server — rejected for the 119-tool duplication. Design 3 (this one) keeps Design 2's mechanism and swaps the target for the filtered endpoint. The enabling facts were verified against the live CLIs before committing: Claude's --mcp-config <configs...> is variadic, accepts inline JSON, and only becomes exclusive under --strict-mcp-config; Codex's dotted -c paths CREATE config entries, including http_headers for the auth token. Codex gains full parity — no ~/.codex/config.toml entry needed anymore, which also defangs the old hardcoded-server-name backlog item.

comments.body: The fallback ladder, in one place: docent-only endpoint → public server URL (unauthenticated, full toolset — only when arming failed) → null (skip injection; the nav notice/balloon explain why). Each rung resolves fresh per launch, so neither the port nor the token can go stale the way a written-once config file entry does — the exact weakness of AWB's own "set up MCP" bubble, which bakes the current port into the user's client config.

If the user themselves enabled AWB's managed wiring (the registry key we chose not to touch), the command already carries --strict-mcp-config plus a merged config pointing at this IDE — the docent tools are reachable through it, and adding a second config under strict semantics has unclear precedence. Standing down is the safe move in a setup that already works.

Verified live before relying on it: codex -c mcp_servers.docent.http_headers.IJ_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN=tok mcp get docent shows the header registered. Codex's mcp add --help only advertises bearer tokens for HTTP servers — the config schema is more capable than the CLI surface suggests. The token value (a UUID) fails TOML parsing and falls back to a literal string, which is exactly what we want.

Demoted from load-bearing to defensive. Before: this HAD to match the user's config.toml entry or Codex never saw the tools. Now the injected docent entry guarantees visibility — but a user entry pointing at the public server also exposes the docent tools, and we can't control which entry Codex resolves a call through, so its 60s timeout still gets lifted to protect a blocking docent_await_event.

Gotcha for future archaeology: the installed AWB 262.8377 has this class under com.intellij.platform.ai.agent…, while the intellij-community checkout still shows it under com.intellij.agent.workbench… — same package split that already moved the session/launch types. Reading the community source will mislead you about import paths.

anchors.label: Why the AWB registry key stays untouched

comments.body: This paragraph replaced its own predecessor twice today. Original: "don't enable direct-http, stdio is the working path" (rationale obsolete — the ~60s HTTP timeout only mattered for blocking docent_await_event, and Claude moved to file-watch delivery). Then briefly: "we flip the key on once". Final: don't touch it at all, at the reviewer's direction — the injection above achieves the same zero-setup result without changing AWB's behavior for everything else.

sections.headline: Follow-up reviews: close the loop with the machinery that already exists
sections.narration: The roughest edge from real use (top of STATUS's "what's left"): after "Complete review" dispatches the queued change requests, the agent edits the code — and that delta, the code the reviewer most explicitly asked to see, landed as a raw diff with no trail and no continuity. The v1 answer deliberately builds no new UI: the agent is now instructed to record a decision per implemented request (what was asked, how it was addressed, where it deviated) and then announce that the delta is reviewable. From there the existing on-demand machinery carries it: fresh decisions repopulate the start surface's pending counts, the user clicks "Start reviewing" again, and the synthesized "Other changes" section absorbs the already-reviewed remainder while the response sections lead. The real UI continuity — a resolved state on the original request card with its edit attached, a baseline snapshot at completion so an uncommitted follow-up diffs against the reviewed state instead of HEAD — is deferred, not rejected: the reviewer said that UX is still a gray area, and release day is the wrong moment to guess it.

comments.body: Of the three places this instruction now lives (envelope hint, launch-injected protocol, tool descriptions), this one is load-bearing: it arrives in the review_completed envelope at the exact moment the agent starts implementing, so it survives the context compaction that may have eaten a launch-time system prompt hours earlier.

sections.headline: Release engineering: reproducible EAP base, first-user README
sections.narration: Two installation-facing changes. Build base: CI used to track the rolling 2026.2-SNAPSHOT because, when that was written, no published EAP matched the Agent Workbench pin — the snapshots repo topped out at EAP6 (262.7581) against a 262.8377 workbench. That gap closed on June 25: EAP8 is build 262.8377.34 (JetBrains skipped EAP7 entirely), an exact three-way match with the local dev base and the AWB pin, so CI is now anchored on it and builds are reproducible instead of drifting until the rolling snapshot breaks compilation. Caveat: local builds resolve the IDE from riderLocalPath, so the download path is only exercised on CI — watch the first run. README: rewritten from a project pitch into a first-user guide (what it does, the five-step review loop, install-from-zip, first run, troubleshooting). Notably, the "turn on the MCP server" first-run step and the "Using Codex? one extra step" section were both written and then deleted again today as the endpoint work made them unnecessary — the first-run list is now: open the panel, launch an agent, click Start reviewing.

comments.body: Verified against JetBrains data services before pinning: 2026.2-EAP8 = build 262.8377.34, exactly the local Rider and the pinned agentWorkbenchVersion (262.8377.20260625). The AWB API differs build-to-build, so this three-way alignment is what makes the pin safe; bump both together, always.
0.4.0 was built and installed mid-session (before the endpoint rework); bumped so install-from-disk replaces it cleanly.

This step absorbed two prerequisites that existed this morning: "turn on the MCP server" (gone — the endpoint doesn't need it) and the Codex config.toml block (gone — injected per launch). If the first wave still stumbles here, the endpoint isn't doing its job.
comments.anchorText: Launch an agent session from the **Agent Workbench** and give it a task.

comments.body: Deliberately honest markers: a previous status pass let stale "not click-tested" claims propagate into other docs and advice, so this one separates what's verified live (everything pre-0.4.0) from today's work, which has only compiler-level and CLI-probe verification behind it.
